title: The apocalypse in art
hookLine: the Angers tapestry, Dürer's woodcuts: artists pictured Revelation vividly
tomorrow: When the saints go marching in

lines: A BOOK MADE FOR THE EYE.
cards: In a castle in the French city of Angers hangs a tapestry of the book of Revelation, woven in wool, so long you see it by walking beside it, scene after scene: angels with trumpets, the dragon, the beast, the holy city coming down.
In Germany, the artist Albrecht Dürer made Revelation into woodcuts and printed it, and his four horsemen gallop off the page together.
Painters, weavers, glassmakers and printers have kept turning this book into pictures. Why does it lend itself to the eye, and what do the pictures uncover?

teach.b: First, the name. The book opens, in the King James, "The Revelation of Jesus Christ." The Greek word there is apokalypsis: an uncovering, an unveiling.
In the text, apocalypse doesn't mean disaster. It means a curtain pulled back. Second, the book is already a picture book.

teach.h: I SAW, I BEHELD, I LOOKED.
teach.b: Again and again John says I saw, I beheld, I looked.

In chapter six, as the seals open, the horses come one by one: white, red, black, and then: "And I looked, and behold a pale horse: and his name that sat on him was Death, and Hell followed with him."
Colors, riders, crowns, scales. An artist barely has to invent anything.
Third, every picture is a reading. Which scene? How frightening?

teach.h: AN IMAGE SENDS YOU TO THE TEXT.
teach.b: Do the horsemen come one by one, as the text has them, or charge together, as Dürer drew them, one wave thundering over the people below? The dragon, or the woman it can't destroy?

Some artists dwelt on the terror; some gave as much room to the river, the tree and the open city. A tapestry or a woodcut shows what its maker heard in the book, and often what the maker's own time feared and hoped.
Fourth, why it matters. A picture can do what the book does: hold back the ordinary for a moment and uncover something.
Some people meet Revelation first through an image, and a pale horse on a print can send a reader to look up chapter six.

how: Christians have pictured Revelation in tapestries, illuminated manuscripts, woodcuts, paintings and stained glass, and some churches and museums display these works for people to look at and pray with.

games.q: what does “the apocalypse in art” mean?
o: modern films about the end of the world
artists turning Revelation's visions into pictures
paintings of real wars and natural disasters

games.q: Revelation in art — tap the pairs.

s: the word apocalypse means the destruction of the world
the book's own word, apokalypsis, means an uncovering: "The Revelation of Jesus Christ."
in Revelation 6, the rider on the pale horse is named Death
"his name that sat on him was Death, and Hell followed with him."
in the text, the four horsemen charge out together
they come one by one, as the seals open. Dürer drew them riding together.

games.q: you're an artist asked to show the pale horse of Revelation 6 to people who can't read. if you follow the text, what must its rider have?
o: the name Death, with Hell following him.
games.why: "his name that sat on him was Death, and Hell followed with him." the bow and crown belong to the white horse's rider; the balances to the black.

practice: Find one image from Revelation, Dürer's Four Horsemen, a panel of the Angers tapestry, a picture in a Bible, or simply picture this week's city with open gates.

Look, without reading about it, until you find one detail you missed at first glance. Then ask what the artist was afraid of, and what the artist hoped for; if you pray, let the image become a prayer without words.

wordCard.voice: The apocalypse in art. Tapestry, woodcut, paint and glass: artists turning John's I saw into pictures, each one a reading of the book.

orig.note: Greek: an uncovering, an unveiling. the first word of the book of Revelation.

carryVoice: Your line: art unveils. Every picture of the book is someone's reading of it. Until tomorrow.
